original_question: What if a rainstorm dropped all of its water in a single giant drop?
short_answer_summary: A kilometer-scale drop from a large storm crashes down and spreads as a destructive supersonic wall of water.
detailed_scientific_explanation: Total precipitable water is the equivalent depth from condensing the atmospheric column. For a100km×100km storm with6cm TPW, water volume is0.6km³ and mass600million tons; condensing it produces a sphere over1km across.

The sphere forms a couple kilometers up. Around10seconds it emerges beneath the cloud, moving90m/s; air strips spray and foams the leading surface. Given enough fall distance it would disperse, but the ground is too near.

About20seconds after formation the edge strikes at over200m/s. Compressed air briefly heats intensely; then impact creates pressures above Mariana Trench conditions and forces water sideways against bedrock as a supersonic radial jet.

Everything within several kilometers is scoured to bedrock. Structures are destroyed20–30km out; terrain begins shielding regions and redirecting water into valleys. Downstream flash floods extend hundreds of kilometers over the following hours. A swimmer in the drop feels little until pressure builds and impact becomes fatal.
initial_assumptions: All moisture becomes one sphere about2km above ground.

quantitative_facts.detail: Impact pressure above Mariana Trench;structures demolished20–30km out;flash floods hundreds ofkm downstream.

footnotes.detail: Footnote celebrates phrase supersonic omnidirectional jet.

uncertainties_and_limitations: Condensation into one stable huge sphere is imposed magic.
Precise breakup and impact not numerically simulated in text.
